title: I inspected all 30,516 remote MCP servers in the official registry
content:
Report · Q4 2026 State of MCP Reliability — Q4 2026 We connected to every remote MCP endpoint in the official MCP Registry, listed its tools, and called none of them. Here is how many actually work, how they break, and what that means for agents and the people who run servers. By Pavel Osadchuk 12 min read Read as Markdown On 20 October 2026 we connected to every remote MCP endpoint in the official MCP Registry: 30,516 URLs. We completed the MCP handshake, asked each server for its tool list, and called no tools. 15,697 servers (51.4%) answered correctly without credentials. 9,517 (31.2%) were up but asked for a key. 3,337 (10.9%) were broken. The handshake is the easy part, though. For 41% of the servers that passed, no tool says whether calling it is safe, so an agent or a monitor has to treat every tool on them as one that can change data. TL;DR # - Snapshot: one inspect (connect + tools/list) of all 30,516 remote endpoints in the official registry, from one vantage point, without credentials. No tool calls. - Status: 51.4% healthy, 31.2% up behind auth, 10.9% broken. The rest were rate-limited by one gateway (4.9%) or asked for payment, HTTP 402 (1.6%). - Rot: listings that were last updated in April 2026 or earlier are broken 40% of the time. Listings updated in October: 4%. - Hosting: Cloudflare Workers endpoints are broken 6% of the time, while Railway and Render endpoints are broken 50% and 39% of the time. Every one of the 190 server.smithery.ai URLs in the registry returns 404. - Auth: 78% of the servers that require a key do not say so in their registry entry. - Safety: one distinct tool in three has no safety hint. Only 7,716 working servers (49%) have a read-only tool that can be called without arguments. - Speed: a healthy server finishes the handshake and the tool list in a median of 1.2 s (p90 3.0 s). - Context: the median tool list is about 2,000 tokens. 741 servers need more than 25,000 tokens before the agent does anything. - Protocols: five protocol versions are in production at the same time. 18.8% of servers already run 2026-07-28. We will run the same scan every quarter and track the same servers over time. Why this report exists # The official MCP Registry grew fast. 64% of its remote listings got their latest version in September or October 2026. A listing says that a server exists. It does not say that the server answers, which tools it has today, or whether those tools still work. Directories and agent platforms show these listings to users as if they all work. Server authors rarely hear about a failure, because an agent that cannot connect does not open an issue. It tries the next server. So we measured it. This is the baseline for a quarterly series that probes the same population again. Method # flowchart TD R[Official MCP Registry: 46,227 active servers] --> U[30,832 unique remote URLs] U -->|316 URL templates skipped| P[30,516 endpoints probed] P --> I[Connect: Streamable HTTP, then legacy SSE] I --> L[tools/list, no tool calls] Three decisions shape these numbers: - Remote endpoints only. A local stdio server has no URL that anyone can probe. We took every active, latest-version entry with a remotes URL and removed duplicates by URL. 316 URLs contain template variables such as {tenant}, so we skipped them. - A real MCP client, inspect only. The probe is the inspect step of MCP Canary, built on the official MCP C# SDK. It tries Streamable HTTP first and falls back to the legacy HTTP+SSE transport on an HTTP 4xx. It negotiates whatever protocol version the server supports. It sends no credentials and never calls a tool: an unknown tool on a stranger's server can send an email or delete a record. - Polite load. At most 2 connections at a time per domain, in random order. An endpoint that timed out or could not be reached got one more try 60 seconds later. 32 endpoints recovered on that retry. What this method misses: it is one snapshot from one place. A server that was down for ten minutes that day counts as broken. And "healthy" means only that the server finished the handshake and listed its tools. It does not mean that the tools work. The headline numbers # Why this is not the 9% you may have seen # An April 2026 scan by AliveMCP of 2,181 endpoints from six sources found 9% healthy. It counted servers that ask for credentials as dead, and it required three passes over three days. Both choices answer a fair question: "can an anonymous agent use this server today?" We answer a different one: "is this server running and speaking MCP?" A server that answers HTTP 401 is running. It wants a token we did not send. Counting it as dead would hide the 9,517 servers that are probably working products behind a login. Bulk publishers do not change the result # The registry has bulk publishers. The ten largest namespaces hold 22% of all endpoints. The largest has 2,365 endpoints, all healthy. Others have hundreds of endpoints that fail in the same way. When we count each of the 18,892 publishers once, the healthy share moves from 51.4% to 49.7%, and the auth share rises from 31.2% to 39.4%. The headline holds. Small publishers put their server behind auth more often. Silent rot: old listings break # The registry stores when each listing's latest version was published. Grouped by that date: Listings that nobody has touched since April are broken 40% of the time. The registry keeps them, marked active, next to servers that work. Two notes: this is the date of the latest version, not of the first release, and active publishers both republish often and keep servers alive. The table shows that untouched listings rot. It does not show how fast a single server dies. The next quarterly scan will measure that directly. Where MCP servers run # Grouped by the hostname of the endpoint: Two groups stand out: - Container platforms with free or credit-based tiers break most often. Half of the Railway endpoints and 39% of the Render endpoints are broken: dead origins (502/503), deleted apps (404), and expired hosts. The pattern fits a project deployed on a trial and then forgotten. - Old hosted URLs stay in the registry. All 190 broken Smithery entries return HTTP 404 at server.smithery.ai. The listings still point there. Workers looks very healthy partly because the largest bulk publisher (2,365 endpoints) runs there and is fully healthy. The seven ways MCP servers break # The 3,337 broken endpoints fail in a few repeating ways. Ranked by count: - Wrong path: HTTP 404 (948). The host is alive, the MCP route is not. 190 of these are the Smithery URLs above. The rest are mostly routes that moved (/mcp to /api/mcp, or a version prefix) without an update to the listing. - Origin down behind a proxy: HTTP 5xx (577). 197 answer 502, 157 answer 503, 107 answer 500, and 114 return Cloudflare's 52x/530 "origin unreachable" errors. A CDN in front of a dead origin still answers, so a ping on the domain stays green. - HTTP alive, MCP broken (559). The server answers but breaks the protocol. 222 fail the new server/discover step of protocol 2026-07-28, most of them by returning a result without the required supportedVersions field. 126 return an empty body to a POST. 95 return a JSON-RPC error to the handshake. 48 send no serverInfo. 36 send invalid JSON. - The domain no longer resolves (539). DNS has no record. Many are project domains that expired. - TLS fails (249). Expired or mismatched certificates. Every modern client refuses the connection. - No answer in 30 seconds (200). The connection hangs. - Other HTTP 4xx (157). Mostly 405 Method Not Allowed (57): the URL serves a web page, not MCP. 49 answer 410 Gone, so the author shut the server down but left the listing. Loud failures and quiet failures # flowchart LR A[Loud
DNS, TLS, refused] --> B[Visible to a ping
5xx, timeouts] B --> C[Quiet
HTTP 200/404/405, but not MCP] C --> D[Silent

report.summary: A scan of all 30,516 remote MCP registry endpoints found only 51.4% healthy, 31.2% behind undeclared auth, and 10.9% outright broken — with stale listings decaying fastest.
report.background: The official MCP Registry grew explosively through 2026: 64% of its remote listings received their latest version in September or October alone, and the registry now holds over 46,000 active servers. But a listing only proves a server was published, not that it answers, still exposes the tools it claims, or that those tools work. Directories and agent platforms surface these entries to users as though every one functions, and server authors rarely learn otherwise — an agent that fails to connect does not file an issue, it silently tries the next server. Previous reliability scans were narrow in scope or counted credential-gated servers as dead, so MCP Canary ran a broad, protocol-level inspection to establish a reproducible quarterly baseline for the ecosystem.
key_points: Of 30,516 remote endpoints probed, 15,697 (51.4%) completed the MCP handshake and returned a tool list without credentials. Another 9,517 (31.2%) were alive but demanded an API key, 3,337 (10.9%) were broken, 4.9% were rate-limited by a single gateway, and 1.6% returned HTTP 402 payment-required. The 51.4% headline differs from an earlier 9% figure mainly because auth-gated servers count as running here.

Listings decay silently: entries last updated in April 2026 or earlier fail 40% of the time, while October updates fail only 4%. Hosting strongly predicts reliability — Cloudflare Workers endpoints break 6% of the time, versus 50% for Railway and 39% for Render, a pattern consistent with trial deployments that were abandoned. All 190 server.smithery.ai URLs in the registry return 404.

Failures cluster into seven repeating modes: wrong path (948, mostly routes that moved without a listing update), dead origin behind a proxy (577), HTTP-alive-but-protocol-broken (559, including 222 that fail the new server/discover step), non-resolving domains (539), TLS failures (249), 30-second timeouts (200), and other 4xx (157). Many stay invisible to simple uptime pings.

Safety metadata is thin: one in three distinct tools carries no safety hint, so an agent must assume it can mutate data. Only 49% of working servers expose a read-only tool callable without arguments, and 78% of auth-requiring servers do not declare that requirement in their registry entry, forcing clients to discover it by failing.

Operational cost matters too. A healthy server completes handshake plus tool listing in a median 1.2 seconds (p90 3.0s), and the median tool list consumes roughly 2,000 tokens of context — but 741 servers burn more than 25,000 tokens before the agent does any work. Five protocol versions run in production simultaneously, with 18.8% already on 2026-07-28.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a maturity check: MCP has real infrastructure, but the registry functions as a catalog, not a health guarantee, and agents now depend on it. Agent platform vendors will likely need to add continuous probing, ranking by liveness, and safety-annotation enforcement, or their products will quietly route around dead servers. Developers building servers should treat listings as living artifacts — republish regularly, declare auth requirements, add read-only tools and annotations, and avoid free-tier hosts for anything meant to stay up. Regular users will mostly feel this as flakiness: a tool that worked last month vanishing without a message. The fix is ecosystem-level observability, not user vigilance.
report.tools: Watch MCP Canary, whose open inspect step produced this data and which will rerun quarterly scans. The official MCP Registry is the source population to query. The MCP C# SDK underpins the probe and is a practical reference client. AliveMCP offers a stricter anonymous-access view that complements this report. If you publish servers, verify your transport against the 2026-07-28 server/discover requirements, add tool safety annotations, and prefer hosting that stays alive after the trial credit runs out.
